<reason>Both sides were disciplined and grounded, but CON made the debate easier to decide. CON seized PRO's "rock cannot leave" line and built a concrete crisis-inventory comparison (producing mine under host sovereignty vs. undeveloped deposit) that PRO never fully dislodged. When PRO answered B's pressure question by naming concrete rebuttal showings (irrevocable allied offtake, audited capital stack, personnel limits), CON convincingly showed those are exactly the mitigation conditions of targeted review, collapsing the dispute to the default under partial disclosure. PRO's remaining route—"title should not move first," burden on the party with the files—stayed live and is a real distinction CON somewhat waved away as "a bad reviewer, not a bad rule," but PRO's own admission that a decade-idle deposit is merely a "commercial cost" was turned against PRO's own crisis-command metric ("nothing commanded in a crisis was started in the crisis"). CON also caught PRO's own "export-license dependence" definition undercutting PRO's narrow reading of "closely tied," which PRO never revisited. CON's late clipping cost little. Clear but competitive win for CON.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's A2 in Rebuttal 2 [B4.3]: showing that PRO's named rebuttal showings [A4.1] are precisely conditioned-review mitigation, so PRO's "reviewer cannot see" objection dissolves and the only difference left is the closing default—paired with the "mines take a decade; crises take weeks" turn on PRO's own metric.</best_rebuttal>
